title: Directed reachability in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space
formal:
Is there one deterministic algorithm that decides directed reachability using polynomial time and polylogarithmic working space simultaneously?

Precisely, does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing decider \(M\) and fixed positive integers \(a,k,c\) such that, for every encoded instance \((G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), it correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), while
\[\operatorname{time}_M(G,s,t)\le c(N+2)^a\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{space}_M(G,s,t)\le c\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil^k?\]
Both bounds must hold for the same computation on every input. This is the question whether directed reachability belongs to the class SC.
why: Directed reachability captures nondeterministic logarithmic space and is a basic model of exploring a large state graph. The question asks whether exploration can be both computationally efficient and extremely economical in reusable memory. Its resolution would clarify the relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic space while separating a genuine simultaneous resource bound from two individually achievable guarantees.

sentences: The problem asks for directed reachability to be decided simultaneously in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space.
One uniform deterministic machine must meet both bounds on every explicitly encoded graph and marked vertex pair.
No graph restrictions, randomness, advice or additional catalytic memory are allowed.
Separate efficient-time and small-space algorithms do not satisfy the joint requirement.
The target is equivalently inclusion of nondeterministic logspace in SC, and is weaker than L equaling NL.

definitions:
For an integer \(v\ge1\), the directed graph \(G=([v],E)\) has \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and \(E\subseteq[v]\times[v]\). Loops are allowed, and repeated edges have no separate meaning. The graph may have cycles, arbitrary in- and out-degree and arbitrarily many paths. No planarity, acyclicity, uniqueness, few-path or connectivity promise is imposed. The marked vertices satisfy \(s,t\in[v]\).

Reachability means that for some integer \(\ell\ge0\) there are vertices \(u_0,\ldots,u_\ell\) with \(u_0=s\), \(u_\ell=t\) and \((u_i,u_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i<\ell\). The zero-edge path makes every vertex reachable from itself. Whenever reachability holds, a path with at most \(v-1\) edges also exists. The required output is one membership bit; a path itself need not be output.

Use the explicit binary encoding \(1^v0\), followed by the \(v^2\) adjacency-matrix bits in row-major order, followed by fixed-width binary encodings of \(s,t\). Each vertex field has \(b_v=\lceil\log_2(v+1)\rceil\) bits and must represent an integer between \(1\) and \(v\). The total length is
\[N=v+1+v^2+2b_v.\]
There are no trailing fields. Any binary string failing this format is rejected. The machine must also meet the same time and space bounds on malformed inputs, measured by their actual length. This representation is polynomially related to the vertex count; it is not a succinct circuit description of an exponentially large graph.

The machine has one two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of ordinary work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, initially blank. Each step changes the finite control, reads or writes a bounded number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Time is the total number of steps until its accept/reject halt, in the worst case. Space is the maximum number of work-tape cells ever visited during the run, multiplied by a fixed number of bits sufficient to encode a tape symbol. In particular all counters, indices, remembered input bits and temporary data count toward space. Input storage and the finite control do not count. The single decision bit is the halting state, so no uncharged output tape can be used as working memory.

No random bits, nondeterministic choices, quantum register, oracle, advice, writable input or extra catalytic memory are available. The same finite program and constants work for all graph orders and all valid and malformed inputs. An algorithm may depend on the fixed encoding, but cannot be chosen separately for each graph. The input is read sequentially by its head rather than supplied as a unit-cost adjacency oracle; scanning it is charged to time.

For an ordinary language of binary strings, SC means decidability by a single uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound and a fixed-power logarithmic space bound as above. It differs from merely supplying one polynomial-time algorithm and another polylogarithmic-space algorithm. The exponent \(k\) is allowed to be any fixed positive integer; the target does not specifically demand logarithmic or squared-logarithmic space.

Equivalently, the question is \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{SC}\). Here NL consists of languages decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine with logarithmic charged work space and a fixed polynomial clock on every branch, accepting an input exactly when at least one branch accepts. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions, and those reductions preserve membership in SC. In particular, \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{NL}\) would imply an affirmative answer, but this card asks only for the weaker simultaneous bounds and does not assert the converse.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the simultaneous-bound existence statement. An affirmative answer must give one exact deterministic decider for all directed graphs and prove its polynomial time and fixed-power logarithmic space bounds with constants independent of the instance. A negative answer must prove that no such decider exists: for every correct uniform decider and every proposed constants, some input violates at least one bound. Separate algorithms meeting separate bounds, a restriction to a special graph family, or a simulation with randomness, advice or catalytic memory is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Exercise 9 explicitly asks whether PATH is in SC and points out that Savitch’s theorem does not settle this. The small-space simulation uses superpolynomial time, while usual graph traversal uses much more than polylogarithmic space.

Barnes, Buss, Ruzzo and Schieber give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with space \(v/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log v})}\). This is sublinear but remains far larger than any fixed power of \(\log v\). Their introduction also separates lower bounds for restricted graph-exploration models from bounds for general Turing computation.

The 2025 paper studies quantum logspace on directed graphs with bounded path counts and reviews deterministic simultaneous bounds for such restricted instances. Its promises and computational model are different from an unrestricted deterministic reachability algorithm.

The February 2026 preprint trades ordinary workspace against an additional tape of catalytic memory. Catalytic storage is extra writable memory that must eventually be restored, and is absent from this card’s model; a small ordinary-workspace bound in that model is not the claimed SC containment.
